passage: I was there when Sahil's flatmates threw him a surprise party for finishing his thesis. He walked in, saw the cake and banner, and his face stayed almost exactly the same. Flat, still. Someone whispered that he seemed unimpressed. I didn't know what to think, because Sahil has told us he's autistic and that his face doesn't always show what he feels. He stood a moment and then said, evenly, "This is the best thing anyone has done for me. Thank you. I'm very happy." I think he was. He also stayed until the end and asked for a second slice. I can't read it from his face, but his words were clear. - Keerthana

qa.q: What did Sahil's flatmates throw for him?
qa.a: They threw him a surprise party for finishing his thesis.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling, given his flat face?
qa.a: He was probably very happy, as he said in words, though his face stayed still, and he told the group his face doesn't always show what he feels.

qa.q: How could the guests find out what Sahil felt?
qa.a: They could listen to his words and ask him, instead of judging from his face.

qa.q: How might the flatmates who planned the party have felt when Sahil's face stayed still?
qa.a: Some of them may have felt unsure or disappointed, as the whisper that Sahil seemed unimpressed suggests, until Sahil said clearly that he was very happy.

grounding: A young adult with a flat facial expression may still feel strongly, and asking and listening to words beats judging feeling from the face.

passage:
Day 1. Hrithik listened to his flatmate Pankaj's plan for a birthday trip without any change in his face. Pankaj felt deflated and thought Hrithik didn't care.
Day 3. Pankaj asked outright, "Do you want to come or not? I can't tell from your face." Hrithik answered, "I'm very excited. I've been looking up train times. My face doesn't move much, but I do feel it strongly. Please ask me in words."
Day 8. They made a habit: Pankaj asked a question, Hrithik answered in a sentence. On the trip, Hrithik said, "This is the best day", his face calm, and Pankaj believed him.

qa.q: What had Hrithik been looking up?
qa.a: He had been looking up train times.

qa.q: What did Pankaj feel on Day 1, and what was Hrithik actually feeling?
qa.a: Pankaj felt deflated, thinking Hrithik didn't care, while Hrithik was very excited but his face didn't show it.

qa.q: What habit did the two make to avoid misunderstanding?
qa.a: Pankaj asks a question and Hrithik answers in a full sentence, so feelings are shared in words, not read from the face.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt when Pankaj said he couldn't tell from his face?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved to be asked directly and given the chance to explain his feelings.

grounding: A young adult with a flat or limited facial expression may still feel strongly, and asking and listening to words beats judging from the face.

passage:
Sarita, you think your new flatmate doesn't like you because her face never changes? Let me, your Lokesh Mama, tell you about Raghu.
Raghu was my closest friend in college. His face hardly moved. When we won the inter-college quiz, the rest of us screamed and jumped. Raghu just stood there, face flat. A senior said, "Your friend doesn't even care."
But on the bus home, Raghu said, very quietly, "This is the best day of my life." I nearly fell off my seat.
Later he told me his face has always been like that, since he was small. "Inside, it's all fireworks," he said. "Outside, it's a wall. People think the wall is me."
After that, I stopped reading his face and started listening to his words. He told me exactly how he felt, if I asked.
So, Sarita, ask your flatmate. Then listen to her words.

qa.q: What did Raghu say on the bus home?
qa.a: "This is the best day of my life."

qa.q: What was Raghu feeling when his face stayed flat after the quiz?
qa.a: Raghu felt overjoyed inside, "all fireworks," even though his face showed nothing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Lokesh Mama's story?
qa.a: Hearing Raghu say it was the best day of his life, which taught Lokesh to stop reading his face and listen to his words.

qa.q: How did the senior read Raghu's flat face?
qa.a: The senior thought Raghu didn't care about winning.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young adult with a flat expression feeling strongly, and a friend learning to ask and listen to words.

passage:
The group presentation was due in two hours, the projector in the seminar room was broken, and Abhinav was losing patience. Bidisha, his partner, had just agreed to present the hardest section, but her face showed nothing. No smile, no nod.
"Are you even okay with this?" Abhinav snapped. "You look like you don't care."
Bidisha paused. "I care a lot. I'm actually excited about this section. I've told people before: my face doesn't show much. It's always been like that. Listen to what I say, not my face."
Abhinav felt his ears go hot. He'd been reading her all semester as bored.
"Sorry. I didn't know."
"Most people don't. Ask me. I'll tell you."
With the projector dead, they printed handouts in the library. In the presentation, Bidisha explained her section with such detail that the professor asked her to lead the next seminar. Her face didn't change. Her words said she was thrilled.

qa.q: How long until the group presentation was due?
qa.a: It was due in two hours.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling about presenting the hardest section?
qa.a: Bidisha felt excited and cared a lot, even though her face showed none of it.

qa.q: What did Abhinav learn to do?
qa.a: To ask Bidisha and listen to her words rather than judge her feelings from her face.

qa.q: How had Abhinav read Bidisha's face all semester?
qa.a: He had read her as bored and uncaring, which was wrong.

grounding: The scene shows a young adult with a limited facial expression feeling strongly, and a partner learning to listen to words under time pressure.

passage:
In their Mumbai office, Gurleen gave Joseph a small birthday gift: a sketchbook with his name embossed on the cover. She'd noticed him drawing in meetings.
Joseph took it, looked at it for a long moment, and said, "Thank you." His face stayed almost exactly the same.
Gurleen's heart sank. He hates it, she thought. She went back to her desk, embarrassed.
An hour later, a message arrived from Joseph. "I want to say more about the sketchbook. I'm autistic, and my face often doesn't show what I feel. I was very happy. Nobody has noticed my drawing before. I already started a page." He attached a photo: a sketch of the office window, with a tiny cartoon of Gurleen waving.
Gurleen laughed out loud and walked over. "I thought you didn't like it."
"I like it a lot," Joseph said, still with his calm face. "Please ask me next time. I'll always tell you."

qa.q: What was embossed on the sketchbook's cover?
qa.a: Joseph's name.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he received the gift?
qa.a: Joseph was very happy and touched that someone had noticed his drawing, even though his face stayed almost the same.

qa.q: What should Gurleen do next time, according to Joseph?
qa.a: Ask him how he feels and listen to his words, since his face often doesn't show his feelings.

qa.q: How did Gurleen first read Joseph's reaction?
qa.a: She thought he hated the gift and felt embarrassed, because his face barely changed.

grounding: The scene shows an autistic young adult with limited facial expression feeling strongly, and a colleague learning to ask and listen to words.

passage:
In the hostel mess, Zeenat waved a printed email over the dal. "I got the exchange semester in Lisbon! Ujjwal, did you hear me?"
Ujjwal looked up from his tray. "I heard. That's big news."
"You said that like you were reading a bus timetable," she said.
"My face doesn't move much. It never has. I'm autistic, and my expressions don't always match what's going on inside."
"So... what is going on inside?"
"A lot. I'm proud of you. I'm also sad, because our Thursday study sessions will end."
"Oh. I honestly thought you didn't care."
"I care. Next time, just ask me, like you did now. Words work better for me than faces."
"Deal. Then I'm telling you in words: I'll miss Thursdays too."
"Good. I'll remember you said it."
Zeenat laughed, and the corner of Ujjwal's mouth lifted into a small, brief smile.

qa.q: Where did Zeenat get an exchange semester?
qa.a: In Lisbon.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling about Zeenat's news, even though his face stayed still?
qa.a: He felt proud of her and also sad that their Thursday study sessions would end; his flat face reflected how his expressions work, not a lack of feeling.

qa.q: What would you advise Zeenat for the next time a friend's face seems blank?
qa.a: Ask and listen to the words, as she finally did with "what is going on inside?", instead of deciding from the face that the friend does not care. 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Zeenat before she asked?
qa.a: She felt hurt and deflated, thinking her big news meant little to Ujjwal.

grounding: It illustrates that an autistic young adult with a flat face can still feel strongly, and that asking and listening to words works better than judging the face.
